transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-01-17 15:00 ET
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Avery Collins (Redwood AE), Diego Marquez (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Horizon Edge CTO), Raj Patel (ML Eng), Samir Khan (Infra), Ella Ramos (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be terse):
Horizon Edge wants a POC to understand per-token costs for their nightly summarization pipeline and a low-latency assistant for sales demos. They are budget-constrained (~$12k/mo target initially) and need p99 latency under 450ms for assistant use. Redwood proposes running a 2-week pilot using a dedicated pool + selective quantized variant for tail reduction; benchmarking will include cache-on vs cache-off runs.

Transcript Body:
[00:00] Avery: hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick intros then we'll jump into the workload, goal is to scope a POC for cost and perf for the summarization plus search assistant.
[00:15] Maya: hi all, Maya here, CTO. we're trying to figure out runway—our finance team gave us a target of about twelve k a month to start for inference, not counting storage.
[00:30] Raj: hey, Raj, ML, i'll bring traffic numbers and sample prompts. currently we batch our nightly summarizer at 10k docs/hour and the interactive assistant sees ~120 concurrent sessions during demos.
[00:48] Diego: quick clarifying q: when you say concurrent sessions, is that steady or spikes during demos?
[00:56] Raj: spikes, usually 300 qps for short windows, typical session length 200–600 tokens. average interactive turn is ~120 tokens.
[01:12] Avery: ok good, so two workloads: async nightly batch where throughput and cost matter, and interactive assistant where latency/p99 matters. success criteria?
[01:26] Maya: p99 under 450ms for assistant, 95% of nightly jobs finish within the 2 hour window. also accuracy on our eval set can't drop more than 2% vs our baseline model.
[01:40] Ella: and data residency concerns — we need logs kept for 90 days and SSO for console access.
[01:48] Avery: noted. we have SOC2 and SSO options, we will send the security pack.
[01:55] Samir: network / infra question: for dedicated we need to know egress and peering requirements. do you support VPC peering?
[02:05] Diego: yes, VPC peering and private deployments are options; for the POC we usually run in a dedicated pool in our hosted environment with customer VPC peering if you want to test end-to-end.
[02:18] Raj: can you give a back-of-envelope per-token cost now? finance wants a number to model.
[02:25] Avery: ballpark yes: for a standard 7B-ish open model hosted path we often show $0.20 to $0.40 per 1k tokens (i.e., $0.0002–$0.0004 per token) depending on batching and cache hit rates. for dedicated and quantized variants that can go down to $0.08–$0.12 per 1k tokens.
[02:49] Maya: that range is big. what's driving the swing?
[02:52] Diego: two main knobs: batching/throughput (more batching increases utilization, lowers unit cost but adds latency) and KV/prefix caching (if assistant reuses context or embeddings, you can avoid recomputing tokens). also quantization reduces GPU hours but can slightly change quality.
[03:10] Raj: whats the typical cache hit rate you see for assistants?
[03:14] Diego: varies—if you have predictable prompts or repeated product docs, 40–70% is realistic. if it's open-ended, closer to 10–20%.
[03:23] Maya: our assistant reuses knowledge often; i think 50% is reasonable.
[03:28] Avery: ok with 50% hit, that shifts effective per-token cost lower; we'll model three scenarios in the spreadsheet.
[03:34] Ella: about benchmarks—what do you need from us?
[03:37] Diego: sample payloads, representative concurrency patterns, and a small eval set for quality regression. we'll run runs with cache enabled/disabled, batching tuned for tail latency, and a quantized variant.
[03:48] Samir: how long does a benchmark take?
[03:50] Diego: depends, but a meaningful run for p99 and throughput is often a 2–4 hour ramp plus some steady-state windows; for stable numbers do at least 3 hours per config. since you have spikes, we'll do a few spike runs.
[04:05] Raj: curious—how do you set batch sizes dynamically? do you have adaptive batching or is it fixed config?
[04:12] Diego: runtime uses continuous batching with latency SLO controls; we can set a max batch window and configure latency targets. for POC we'll try two profiles: low-latency (tight batch, higher cost) and cost-optimized (looser batch).
[04:24] Maya: and quantization—if we use int8 or int4 variants, what's the perf delta?
[04:29] Diego: quantized models can get 2–3x throughput depending on hardware, sometimes at modest quality delta; we'll surface the eval metrics. recommended is to test both quantized and fp16/32 fallbacks for sensitive queries.
[04:42] Raj: what about model fallbacks? if quantized generates weird hallucinations we need automatic fallback to a higher-precision variant.
[04:49] Avery: we support fallback policies—can route by probability/confidence thresholds or by error-rates; during the pilot we can enable logging and automatic fallback for your eval-critical flows.
[04:59] Maya: timeline—can we do this POC within 2 weeks? finance wants results quickly.
[05:05] Diego: yes, typical POC: week 1 instrument + sample data + smoke runs, week 2 full benchmarks and analysis. we'll need your prompt set and access to a staging endpoint by early next week.
[05:18] Samir: about cost modeling, can you include a scenario with burst capacity? during demos we have short 300 qps burst windows.
[05:25] Avery: yes we'll model steady-state and burst using reserved + burst pool; show expected monthly cost with 5 big spikes/month.
[05:33] Ella: what are pass/fail criteria?
[05:35] Avery: propose: (1) p99 assistant latency <450ms for low-latency profile during demo-like spikes, (2) nightly summarizer completes within 2 hours at cost <= $X (we'll compute), (3) quality regression <2% on your eval set. if all pass then we recommend moving to a 3-month paid pilot or Dedicated reserve.
[05:56] Maya: agreed. finance will review the numbers; product approves if quality holds.
[06:02] Raj: on instrumentation—what logs and metrics will you provide?
[06:06] Diego: token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency percentiles, cache hit ratios, and KV cache metrics. we'll share dashboards and a CSV export.
[06:16] Maya: need RBAC for console and request audit logs are mandatory.
[06:20] Avery: included in the security pack; we'll flag retention windows and SSO config.
[06:25] Ella: any competitors we should watch for? we are also talking to a managed endpoint vendor but their benchmarks look higher on per-token.
[06:33] Avery: ok noted. we'll make the spreadsheet transparent so you can compare.
[06:38] Raj: one more—how do you handle mixed workloads? we have both long contexts for summarization and short assistant turns.
[06:44] Diego: we can route by policy—summarization jobs go to cost-optimized pools with large batch windows; interactive assistant goes to latency-optimized pools. same model family, different runtime configs.
[06:55] Maya: what about peak capacity cost—if we hit a festival of demos month, does cost balloon linearly?
[07:00] Avery: yes it's usage-based. reserved capacity smooths cost; for spikes we can autoscale but cost increases. we'll show committed vs on-demand tradeoffs.
[07:09] Raj: ok sounds good. next steps?
[07:12] Avery: action items recap: we'll send the pricing workbook and benchmark plan; Diego will own the runs; Raj and Samir will provide sample data and staging access; Maya/Ella will review security docs.
[07:24] Maya: thanks, speak soon.

End of meeting.
